section_title: Can Saul obtain a different answer by seeking Samuel through a medium?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 7 Then Saul said to his servants, “Find me a woman who is a medium, so I can go and consult her.” “There is a medium at Endor,” his servants replied. 8 So Saul disguised himself by putting on different clothes, and he set out with two of his men. They came to the woman at night, and Saul said, “Consult a spirit for me. Bring up for me the one I name.” 9 But the woman replied, “Surely you know what Saul has done, how he has killed the mediums and spiritists in the land. Why have you set a trap to get me killed?” 10 Then Saul swore to her by the LORD: “As surely as the LORD lives, no punishment shall come upon you for this.” 11 “Whom shall I bring up for you?” the woman asked. “Bring up Samuel,” he replied.

12 But when the woman saw Samuel, she cried out in a loud voice and said to Saul, “Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!” 13 “Do not be afraid,” the king replied. “What do you see?” “I see a god coming up out of the earth,” the woman answered. 14 “What does he look like?” asked Saul. “An old man is coming up,” she replied. “And he is wearing a robe.” So Saul knew that it was Samuel, and he bowed facedown in reverence.

15 Then Samuel said to Saul, “Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?” “I am deeply distressed,” replied Saul. “The Philistines are fighting against me, and God has turned away from me. He no longer answers me, either by prophets or by dreams. So I have called on you to tell me what to do.” 16 “Why do you consult me,” asked Samuel, “since the LORD has turned away from you and become your enemy? 17 He has done exactly what He spoke through me: The LORD has torn the kingdom out of your hand and given it to your neighbor David. 18 Because you did not obey the LORD or carry out His burning anger against Amalek, the LORD has done this to you today. 19 Moreover, the LORD will deliver Israel with you into the hand of the Philistines, and tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. And the LORD will deliver the army of Israel into the hand of the Philistines.”

20 Immediately Saul fell flat on the ground, terrified by the words of Samuel. And his strength was gone, because he had not eaten anything all that day and night. 21 When the woman came to Saul and saw how distraught he was, she said to him, “Look, your maidservant has obeyed your voice. I took my life in my hands and did as you told me. 22 Now please listen to your servant and let me set a morsel of bread before you so you may eat and have the strength to go on your way.” 23 Saul refused, saying, “I will not eat.” But his servants joined the woman in urging him, and he heeded their voice. He got up from the ground and sat on the bed. 24 The woman had a fattened calf at her house, and she quickly slaughtered it. She also took flour, kneaded it, and baked unleavened bread. 25 She served it to Saul and his servants, and they ate. And that night they got up and left.

context_lines: Saul seeks a medium at Endor, disguises himself and goes with two men at night. The woman fears a trap because Saul has acted against mediums and spiritists. He swears by the LORD that she will not be punished, then asks her to bring up Samuel.

The narrative calls the figure Samuel. The woman cries out when she sees him and recognizes Saul. She describes an old man wearing a robe, and Saul bows facedown. Her phrase translated a god uses elohim (eh-loh-HEEM). [Brown–Driver–Briggs](https://biblehub.com/hebrew/430.htm) lists this verse under a godlike being, referring to Samuel’s departed spirit. The word here does not by itself identify the figure as God.

Samuel’s message gives Saul no new way around the earlier judgment. The kingdom has been taken from him and given to David because he did not obey the LORD concerning Amalek. He is told that Israel will fall to the Philistines and that he and his sons will join Samuel in death.

Saul falls to the ground in terror, weakened also by having eaten nothing all day and night. The woman and his servants persuade him to eat. She prepares a calf and unleavened bread, and they leave that night. The scene ends with food and human care, while the announced judgment remains.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-samuel/) and [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_samuel/28.htm) understand the appearance as the real Samuel, whom God permits to appear beyond the woman’s control. They give weight to the narrative naming him and to the woman’s surprise. This reading does not treat the encounter as permission to consult the dead.

[Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/28.htm) favors a deceptive spirit appearing in Samuel’s likeness. He reasons that God would not answer through a forbidden practice after withholding an answer by the appointed means. He acknowledges the force of the text’s naming Samuel, but interprets the scene as an appearance Saul takes to be the prophet. The disagreement concerns the identity and manner of the appearance, not the fact that Saul has sought a forbidden source of guidance.

[Deuteronomy 18:9–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/deuteronomy/18.htm) directly forbids consulting mediums, spiritists and the dead. Saul’s oath to protect the woman does not reverse that instruction. The encounter brings the judgment he wished to escape rather than an alternative plan for winning the battle.

[Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_samuel/28.htm) takes the words about being with Samuel as entry into the world of the dead. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-samuel/) allows a hopeful reading but also says the words may concern death alone. They do not settle Saul’s eternal state simply by placing him, his sons and Samuel in the same sentence.

[Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_samuel/28.htm) warns against despair while urging any reader still willing to repent to seek God’s mercy. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-samuel/) cautions against claiming certainty about contrition the account does not record. The chapter’s silence about Saul’s inner response leaves more unanswered than the description of his fear.
god_plan_lines: The encounter shows that seeking extraordinary access cannot make God’s already spoken word disappear. Saul wants direction for danger, but the answer returns to the obedience he had refused. The [USCCB Bible notes](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/1samuel/28) likewise connect the scene with God’s continuing purpose for David.

The larger biblical movement directs attention to the One through whom God speaks fully. [Hebrews 1:1–4](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/1.htm) traces God’s speech through the prophets to His Son, who reveals His glory, provides purification for sins and sits at His right hand. The Christian response is to receive God’s revelation in Christ, rather than seek a method of controlling the answer.

This is a shared theme of hearing God’s word, not a claim that Hebrews directly explains the mechanics at Endor. The passage’s importance for God’s plan lies in the word that stands and the kingship moving toward David, rather than in satisfying every curiosity about the unseen world.
